questions.q: What does the author compare social media success to?
a: A sport you must train for seriously if you want to go pro
A lottery that rewards whoever posts most often
A dinner party where manners matter most
A shop window that only needs occasional updates
questions.why: Lesson 1 uses the losing softball team to show that a hobby approach will not produce results.

questions.q: What profile changes does the summary recommend?
a: Use your full name and a clear photo of your smiling face
Use a memorable nickname and an artistic avatar
Keep your account anonymous to protect privacy
Post only professional logos instead of photos
questions.why: Lesson 1 advises dropping joke handles and using your real name and a friendly, recognizable picture.

questions.q: What content mix does the summary recommend?
a: Combine your own perspective with things your audience already wants to see
Post only your opinions so your voice stands out
Share only viral articles from other accounts
Publish the same promotional message every day
questions.why: Lesson 2 says to mix your unique view with content people are already discussing and sharing.

questions.q: How many social accounts does the summary suggest managing?
a: Two, or at most three, so you can cross-promote without burning out
As many as possible to reach every platform
One, so your message stays consistent
Five, one for each content format
questions.why: Lesson 3 warns that signing up for ten platforms leads to overwhelm and recommends two or three.

questions.q: What is the point of letting your accounts talk to each other?
a: Driving your audience from one platform to another
Keeping each audience completely separate
Testing which platform performs worst
Automating identical posts everywhere
questions.why: Lesson 3 recommends using every chance to cross-promote so your audience grows faster.
